intro: Each mark stands for one letter. You break a cipher the way you break a case: wait for the tell, then press. No mathematics. Just English, black coffee, and a sharp eye.

tools.body: Shrink the cipher tiles when the quote is crowding the page.
Magnify the tiles when a glyph is hard to read.
Test the highlighted guess. A correct letter locks in; a wrong one takes the red circle. Three checks per edition, shared by the morning and night extras; the count sits on the quill.
Reveal the highlighted glyph. Select a mark first. Three hints per edition, shared by the morning and night extras; the count sits on the bulb.

Open a worksheet of repeating glyphs, busiest first: how often each appears, how often it starts a word, and how often it sits doubled. Counts only; the letters are yours. English leans on E, T, A, O, I, N.
Wipe every guess and start the quote over. The timer keeps running.

tactics.title: Attack the Single-Letter Words First
tactics.summary: English has only two common one-letter words: A and I.

points.body: A standalone glyph is a 50/50 between A and I.
A and I cover nearly every puzzle. O appears as a word in poetry, but rarely here.
If that single letter opens the sentence, it is frequently I.
Morning keeps A as one glyph. Night Extra splits A across two, so a second one-letter word with a different mark can still be A.

tactics.title: Hunt for the Most Frequent Letters
tactics.summary: The letters that dominate English are E, T, A, O, I, N, S, H, R, D, L, and U.

points.body: The leader is very likely E or T.
A glyph that shows up once or twice is probably Z, Q, X, J, or K.

Morning Edition uses one glyph per letter, so counting works. Night Extra gives E, T, and A two glyphs each; every other letter stays one-to-one. The busiest marks are still E or T, just split across a pair.

tactics.title: Spot Common Two- and Three-Letter Words
tactics.summary: Short words are the mortar between nouns and verbs, and only a few are common.

points.body: OF, TO, IN, IT, IS, BE, AS, AT, SO, WE, HE, BY, OR, ON, DO, IF, ME, MY, UP.
THE is the most common, then AND, FOR, WAS, HIS, NOT.
If a frequent three-letter word starts with a letter you already think is I or A, you may be looking at THE or AND.
Night Extra splits T and E, so THE can show up as two glyph patterns that share the same middle mark for H.

tactics.title: Look for Apostrophes
tactics.summary: An apostrophe sharply limits which letters can follow it.

points.body: Almost always S, T, D, or M (IT'S, CAN'T, YOU'D, I'M).
Usually RE, VE, or LL (THEY'RE, WE'VE, YOU'LL).
If the word ends in N'T, you have just solved N and T.
N'T still solves N on both editions. Night Extra splits T, so the mark after the apostrophe is only one of the two T glyphs.

tactics.title: Identify Double Letters
tactics.summary: Twin glyphs give away the shape of a word.

points.body: LL, SS, TT, FF, RR, NN, PP, CC.
EE and OO.
At the end of a word, often LL or SS. In the middle of a short word, often EE or OO (SEEN, GOOD).
Morning doubles always match. Night Extra splits E and T, so EE and TT may look like two marks. OO, LL, and SS still pair.

charter.title: The Bureau's Rules of Fair Play
charter.summary: Every agent is owed a fair page. These are the terms the Bureau holds its press to before a page is set.

points.body: Every page is written to be read from what is in front of you: the cipher, its article, and the pages you have already decoded.
Where the last word of a line could be read two ways, the article or plain grammar settles it. The press checks every page for such a word before it runs.
A harder page is harder by a rule this Handbook states, never by one it keeps back. Night Extras split E, T and A, and nothing else.
The desk never says a guess is right or wrong until you spend a check. The page stamps itself when every mark is right.
Hints and checks are rationed and printed on your result. A clean page is one decoded without either.

nightMemo.title: Memorandum: The Night Desk
nightMemo.body: Night Extras come off a different machine. E, T and A each print as one of two marks, used in turn; every other letter keeps its single mark. Count as you always have, but pair the busiest marks: two of them may be the same letter. The Handbook has the full procedure under each tell.
